actions.justification: Mandatory first step - continuous vital sign monitoring is required for any patient with acute dyspnea and chest pain to establish hemodynamic stability and guide further management.

Mandatory - Wells score is the standard clinical pre-test probability tool for PE, which is the leading diagnosis given pleuritic chest pain and acute dyspnea. This guides the diagnostic pathway (D-dimer vs. direct CT-PA).
Mandatory - D-dimer is a key diagnostic test in the PE workup. If Wells score is low-to-intermediate, a negative D-dimer can exclude PE without imaging. Must be ordered early.

A 12-lead ECG is a Class I recommendation within 10 minutes of presentation for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI, right heart strain pattern (S1Q3T3), or other arrhythmias that may accompany pulmonary embolism or other cardiopulmonary diagnoses.
Patient presents with acute dyspnea. Supplemental oxygen should be provided as a supportive measure to maintain adequate oxygenation during the diagnostic workup, even with SpO2 currently at 98%.

Given the presentation of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with pending D-dimer and Wells score already assessed, early pulmonology consultation is appropriate to assist with workup and management of suspected pulmonary embolism or other pulmonary pathology.

CT Pulmonary Angiography is the gold standard for diagnosing pulmonary embolism in this patient presenting with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with elevated clinical suspicion (Wells score already assessed). This is the definitive diagnostic test for PE.
Chest X-ray should be obtained to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) and to assess baseline cardiopulmonary status per AHA chest pain guidelines.

Echocardiogram is indicated to assess for right ventricular strain/dysfunction, which would risk-stratify this patient and help determine if high-risk PE management (thrombolysis) is needed, particularly if CT-PA confirms PE.

A 12-lead ECG is indicated per AHA guidelines for acute chest pain evaluation. Although an ECG was previously ordered (order_ecg), order_imaging_ecg is a distinct action_id in the available list and should be completed to ensure cardiac causes (STEMI, right heart strain pattern suggesting PE) are fully evaluated.

Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound is indicated in the workup of suspected pulmonary embolism (pleuritic chest pain, acute dyspnea) to identify deep vein thrombosis, which would support the diagnosis and guide anticoagulation decisions.

Echocardiogram can assess for right heart strain, elevated pulmonary artery pressure, and right ventricular dysfunction, which are critical for risk stratification in suspected PE and to guide management decisions.

ABG is indicated to assess oxygenation, ventilation status, and acid-base balance in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, which may represent pulmonary embolism. Helps evaluate severity and guides management.
BNP helps assess right heart strain, which would be relevant if PE is confirmed, aiding risk stratification (massive vs submassive PE).
Basic metabolic panel provides baseline renal function (important before contrast CT-PA if not yet completed) and electrolyte status to guide overall management.
CBC is needed to assess baseline hemoglobin/hematocrit, platelet count before initiating anticoagulation therapy for suspected PE, and to evaluate for anemia or infection.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are essential baseline labs before initiating anticoagulation therapy for suspected PE, and to evaluate for any underlying coagulopathy.
Lactate level helps assess hemodynamic stability and tissue perfusion, useful for risk stratification in suspected PE to determine if there is evidence of shock/hemodynamic compromise.

Cardiac troponin is indicated for risk stratification of pulmonary embolism. Elevated troponin suggests myocardial injury from right ventricular strain and would classify this as intermediate-high risk PE, influencing management decisions. This is a standard component of PE workup that has not yet been completed.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, highly suspicious for pulmonary embolism. Extensive workup including CT-PA, D-dimer, Wells score, and lower extremity Doppler has been ordered. While awaiting confirmation, empiric anticoagulation is indicated given high clinical suspicion for PE, stable hemodynamics (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), and no apparent contraindications. Early anticoagulation reduces thrombus propagation and mortality risk in suspected PE per guidelines.

In suspected/confirmed PE, interventional radiology consultation is appropriate for catheter-directed therapy planning, particularly if CT-PA shows significant clot burden. This prepares the team for escalation if needed.

Supportive IV fluid administration is appropriate in PE management to maintain preload and hemodynamic stability while awaiting pending diagnostic results, as long as the patient does not have signs of right heart failure (echo pending).

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, consistent with pulmonary embolism. CT-PA and D-dimer have been ordered; anticoagulation with heparin is indicated for suspected/confirmed PE to prevent clot propagation while awaiting full diagnostic confirmation. Heparin (UFH) is appropriate given stable hemodynamics (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%).

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with a working diagnosis consistent with pulmonary embolism. Heparin has been given but LMWH (low molecular weight heparin) represents appropriate anticoagulation therapy for confirmed or high-probability PE. This is the only clinically relevant available action given that assessment and diagnostics are already completed, vasopressors are not indicated (hemodynamically stable, MAP 78, HR 80), and thrombolysis is not indicated without massive PE criteria (hemodynamically stable).
